title: Spinning from flicked locks
subtitle: Preparing individual wool locks with a flicker brush before spinning
excerpt: Flicking individual locks with a flicker brush opens the cut and tip ends without combing the whole lock into a top. It is faster than full combing, preserves lock length, and suits medium breeds like Corriedale or Down crosses. The resulting preparation spins semi-worsted.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from standard guild workshop practice for lock-by-lock wool preparation. The flicker brush technique is a practical home alternative to full hand-combing for medium and long-staple breeds.

glossaryTerms.definition: The length of an individual wool lock from cut end to tip.
A preparation method for individual wool locks using a stiff-bristled flicker brush. Each end of the lock is flicked open to remove vm and tangles without full combing.

attrs.title: Wool dust
attrs.body: Flicking releases fibre dust and VM particles. Work in a ventilated space and damp-mop the floor when done.

items.name: Washed wool fleece with intact locks

content.text: Hold the lock near its tip end with the cut end hanging free. Rest the cut end against the palm of the holding hand or against your knee with a leather pad for protection. Flick the brush downward through the cut end two or three times with a quick wrist snap. The matted cut end will open into a fan of loose fibres. Stop once the fibres are open; over-flicking shortens the lock and blurs the worsted alignment.

Transfer the lock so the tip end hangs free. Flick the tip end in the same way. The tip is often more matted than the cut end because it has been exposed to weather; it may need three or four flicks to open fully. If the tip is heavily felted (the fibres have matted together rather than just lying in a clump), the lock is from a fleece that has been stored too long and may draft poorly. Discard heavily felted tips.

Hold the flicked lock by one end and present the other end to the wheel orifice. Draft with a semi-worsted draw: allow twist to run up to the front hand, then release to draw back. The flicked lock drafts in one direction only: from the open flicked end backward into the body of the lock. Spinning from tip to cut or cut to tip gives different surface results; most spinners prefer cut to tip for a slightly smoother yarn.

items.problem: The lock keeps pulling apart while drafting
items.cause: The lock was over-flicked or the fibres were already short due to lock damage or breakage
items.fix: Check the raw fleece for weak spots by pulling a small amount of the lock sharply: a sound lock resists the pull. Avoid flicking more than three to four times per end.

items.problem: VM falls out onto the wheel and yarn
items.cause: The flicking only opened the ends; heavy VM in the mid-lock remains until it reaches the orifice
items.fix: For heavily VM-loaded fleece, pick the locks by hand to remove obvious seeds and chaff before flicking. The flicker brush is most effective on clean or lightly soiled fleece.
